title: DevSecOps Implementation: Integrate Security Into Delivery
description: A practical DevSecOps implementation guide for threat modeling, code and dependency checks, secrets, CI/CD permissions, release gates, and measurable remediation.
author: PilotStack Editorial Team

sections.title: Start With the Delivery Path
sections.body: Map how code moves from a developer's workstation through review, build, test, artifact storage, deployment, and production monitoring. Identify where credentials are used, where third-party dependencies enter, and which steps can change production. Choose security controls based on the risks in this path rather than adding every scanner at once. Assign an owner for each control and define how exceptions are approved. Security becomes sustainable when it is part of the normal delivery workflow and the people who receive findings can act on them.

sections.title: Prioritize Threats and Controls
sections.body: Use the application's data, trust boundaries, exposure, and business impact to identify likely threats. Consider unauthorized access, injection, dependency compromise, leaked secrets, insecure configuration, and deployment abuse. Map each important threat to a preventive or detective control and a test that demonstrates the control works. A scanner finding is useful evidence, but it is not a substitute for understanding the threat model. Revisit the model when architecture, permissions, data sensitivity, or external integrations change.

sections.title: Secure Source and Build Pipelines
sections.body: Review the delivery pipeline for the controls that prevent an untrusted change from reaching production.
items: Require review for sensitive code and protect release branches.
Use short-lived or scoped credentials instead of broad long-lived tokens where possible.
Separate build permissions from deployment permissions.
Pin or verify dependencies and protect artifact provenance.
Run secret detection and prevent credentials from being committed.
Limit access to CI variables, logs, artifacts, and production environments.
Keep rollback procedures and deployment approvals documented.

sections.title: Use Security Tests With Clear Ownership
sections.body: Select static analysis, dependency checks, secret detection, infrastructure checks, and dynamic tests according to the application's architecture and risk. Decide which findings block a release and which create tracked remediation work. Avoid a gate that fails builds for large volumes of low-confidence findings without a triage process. Route findings to code owners with severity, affected component, reproduction guidance, and a remediation deadline. Measure whether important issues are resolved, not just how many scans ran.

sections.title: Manage Secrets and Supply-Chain Risk
sections.body: Store secrets in an approved secret manager, scope them to the task, and rotate them after exposure. Treat CI logs and build artifacts as potential leakage paths. Inventory direct and transitive dependencies, review update sources, and document how vulnerable components are assessed. For critical artifacts, verify where they came from and whether the release process was authorized. Maintain a process for urgent dependency fixes that balances speed with validation and rollback.

sections.title: Prepare for Production and Incidents
sections.body: Define production permissions, environment separation, logging, alerting, and the process for revoking access during an incident. Ensure that a deployment can be rolled back and that a responder can identify the code and dependencies in a release. Link security alerts to the team that owns the service, and keep a runbook for common incidents such as a leaked token or a vulnerable dependency. Test the response path periodically so the team does not discover missing permissions or stale documentation during a real incident.

sections.title: Measure the Program and Improve It
sections.body: Track a small set of operational indicators: time to remediate critical findings, percentage of repositories with required controls, secret incidents, dependency exposure, and the number of exceptions past due. Interpret these metrics alongside the risk and size of the systems involved. Review false positives and developer friction so controls remain effective without creating workarounds. Assign owners and dates to improvements, then revisit the threat model and pipeline when the delivery process changes.
